lessons.title: Types of plant manipulation
lessons.html:
What is plant manipulation?

Plant manipulation means actions that change how a plant grows to improve yield, quality, timing or ease of management. Supervisors must know the purpose of each practice so they can check that teams do it correctly.

Common practices

PracticePurposeExamples
PruningShape the plant, remove dead or diseased wood, let light in, balance growth and fruitingGrapevines, citrus, stone fruit, apples
Training and trellisingGuide growth onto supports for light, airflow and easier harvestVines on wires, tomatoes on strings, espalier apples
ThinningRemove some fruit or seedlings so the rest grow bigger and betterPeaches, plums, apples, carrots, beetroot
Topping and pinchingStop upward growth and encourage side shoots or fruitTomatoes, cotton, tobacco, herbs
Side-shooting (suckering)Remove unwanted shoots to focus energyIndeterminate tomatoes, citrus rootstock suckers
DeleafingImprove airflow and light to fruit, reduce diseaseTunnel tomatoes, grapes
Girdling or ringingImprove fruit set or size in some crops, done strictly to specificationSome table grapes and citrus
Growth regulatorsChange growth, fruit set, ripening or sizeApplied per label and adviser's programme only
Pollination supportEnsure fruit setHiring beehives for orchards, hand pollination

Timing

Each practice has a correct time. Winter pruning of deciduous fruit takes place in dormancy; summer pruning controls vigour. Thinning is done early, before the fruit uses too much energy. Late or early work can reduce yield.

Hygiene

Pruning cuts are entry points for disease. Use sharp, clean tools, disinfect between blocks or diseased plants as instructed, and remove diseased prunings from the orchard.

lessons.title: Monitoring the quality of manipulation work
lessons.html:
Setting the standard

Before work starts, make sure the team understands the specification for the block. For example: "Thin peaches to one fruit every 15 cm on the shoot," or "Leave two spurs with two buds each." Demonstrate on a few plants, then let each worker try while you watch.

What to check during work

  • Are cuts clean, at the correct position (e.g. just above a bud, at the correct angle) and without tearing bark?
  • Is the number of fruit, buds, shoots or leaves left within specification?
  • Are workers using the correct tools and PPE (gloves, eye protection, safe ladders)?
  • Is diseased material removed and handled correctly?
  • Is the pace realistic without sacrificing quality?

Sampling method

Check a fixed number of plants per worker or per row, chosen across the block. Count, for example, fruits left per shoot or buds per spur, and record the results. If more than an agreed percentage is out of specification, stop, retrain and rework.

Records

Record date, block, practice, workers or team, number of plants done, quality check results and corrective actions. Records help managers link practices to later yield and quality.

Monitoring plant response

Return later to check results: new shoot growth, fruit set, fruit size, disease levels and sunburn. Report unexpected responses, such as excessive regrowth or fruit drop, to the manager or adviser.

Safety

  • Ladders must be stable and on firm ground; never overreach.
  • Secateurs and pruning saws are sharp: keep the free hand clear.
  • Powered pruners and chainsaws need training and PPE.
  • Growth regulators and sprays must only be applied by trained workers following the label and the farm's programme.

Key points

  • Plant manipulation includes pruning, training, thinning, topping, deleafing and growth regulators.
  • Each practice has a purpose, specification and correct timing.
  • Demonstrate the standard and check samples during work.
  • Record work done and quality results.
  • Use safe ladders, sharp clean tools and the right PPE.
